outline.chapter_title: Foundation Models and the Need for Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
outline.description: This opening chapter motivates the problem addressed by the paper. It introduces the rise of large foundation models, explains why full retraining is often impractical, and situates BOFT within the broader landscape of parameter-efficient finetuning.
subtopics: Why foundation models are powerful but expensive to train from scratch
Downstream adaptation as a central problem in modern machine learning
The three main PEFT families: model finetuning, adapter tuning, and prompt tuning
Why model finetuning is attractive: simplicity and no added inference latency
The core challenge of preserving pretrained knowledge during adaptation
Additive updates versus multiplicative updates in finetuning
Low-rank structure and sparse structure as two routes to parameter efficiency
High-level overview of OFT and BOFT
The paper's main contributions and what makes BOFT new

outline.description: This chapter builds the mathematical intuition behind Orthogonal Finetuning. It explains why orthogonal transformations are a principled way to adapt pretrained weights while preserving important geometric relationships among neurons.
subtopics: Review of linear layers and weight matrices in neural networks
Viewing columns of a weight matrix as neurons
Pairwise angles between neurons as relational information
Orthogonal matrices and their geometry-preserving properties
Why preserving neuron angles can help retain pretrained semantics
The OFT update rule: replacing W0 with R W0
Identity initialization as a way to start from the exact pretrained model
Skew-symmetric matrices and the Cayley parameterization
How Cayley transforms enforce orthogonality during training
Conceptual comparison between OFT and LoRA

outline.chapter_title: Why OFT Still Uses Too Many Parameters
outline.description: Although OFT is principled and effective, its orthogonal matrix can still be too large to train efficiently. This chapter explains the parameter bottleneck, the block-diagonal workaround used in prior OFT, and the limitations that motivate BOFT.
subtopics: Parameter cost of a dense d-by-d orthogonal matrix
Why naive OFT scales poorly in high dimensions
Block-diagonal orthogonal matrices as the original OFT solution
How block size controls the parameter-efficiency trade-off
Independent transformations across blocks and the resulting inductive bias
Why grouping dimensions by index is hard to justify
Reduced expressivity caused by fixed sparsity patterns
Why block-diagonal OFT cannot recover many classic dense linear transforms
The central design goal: dense orthogonal updates with far fewer parameters

outline.description: This chapter presents the paper's key conceptual shift: understanding sparse matrix factorization as an information transmission problem on a graph. This viewpoint makes the search for efficient orthogonal parameterizations much more intuitive.
subtopics: Factoring a dense transform as R = B_m ... B_1
Unrolling matrix multiplication into a grid-structured graph
Interpreting nonzero matrix entries as edges that transmit information
Dense matrices as all-to-all reachability between source and destination nodes
How reachability determines the sparsity pattern of a product matrix
Reading missing connections from partial products
Why orthogonality constrains allowable edge patterns
Necessary edges versus trainable or free edges
The two main desiderata: dense connectivity and minimum free edges
Trading computation for memory through repeated sparse multiplications
Why this framework is especially useful for studying OFT-style updates

outline.chapter_title: Butterfly Structures and Efficient Dense Connectivity
outline.description: Having framed the problem as information transmission, this chapter introduces butterfly structures as a near-ideal topology for sparse yet expressive connectivity. It connects BOFT to fast transforms such as the FFT and shows why butterfly factorization is so parameter-efficient.
subtopics: The Cooley-Tukey FFT and the origin of butterfly graphs
Why butterfly networks are efficient communication topologies
Defining a butterfly factor
Recursive construction of butterfly matrices
Butterfly components as structured sparse block matrices
The block-butterfly generalization used in the paper
How butterfly factorization achieves dense connectivity with O(d log d) structure
Comparison with a single dense matrix and with block-diagonal sparsity
Why butterfly structure can recover many classic fast linear transforms
Prior uses of butterfly matrices in numerical methods and machine learning

outline.description: This chapter develops the paper's main method. It shows how to turn butterfly factorization into an orthogonal parameterization, how BOFT is inserted into a pretrained model, and how its special cases recover earlier OFT variants.
subtopics: Making each butterfly component orthogonal
Orthogonal 2-by-2 rotations and their blockwise generalization
Using Cayley parameterization inside butterfly blocks
Constructing the final BOFT transform R(m, b)
The BOFT forward pass for a pretrained linear layer
Notation for block size, number of factors, and model variants
Special case: BOFT with one factor equals block-diagonal OFT
Special case: BOFT with one full block equals unconstrained OFT
Special case: enough butterfly factors yields a dense orthogonal matrix
Effective parameter count and why BOFT scales as O(d log d) in the butterfly setting
How BOFT generalizes OFT into a broader orthogonal finetuning framework

outline.description: This chapter focuses on the practical side of using BOFT. It covers initialization, regularization, parameter budgeting, and the computational trade-offs that arise when replacing one large matrix with multiple sparse orthogonal factors.
subtopics: Identity initialization for all butterfly components
Why identity initialization preserves the exact pretrained model at step zero
Why standard dropout does not directly fit multiplicative orthogonal updates

Choosing the number of factors m and block size b
Balancing expressivity, regularity, and parameter budget
Computation-versus-memory trade-offs in repeated sparse multiplications
Training stability considerations for orthogonal updates
How BOFT can be merged into pretrained weights after finetuning
Why BOFT adds no inference latency despite extra training-time structure

outline.description: This chapter develops the paper's main theoretical and conceptual insights. It explains why BOFT is more expressive than block-diagonal OFT, why orthogonal updates are stable, and how structured sparsity can act as a beneficial inductive bias.
subtopics: Simulation-based approximation of random orthogonal matrices

outline.chapter_title: Empirical Validation Across Vision, Language, and Generation
outline.description: This chapter explains the paper's experimental program and main empirical findings. It highlights how BOFT was evaluated across multiple model families and task domains, and what these experiments show about parameter efficiency, generalization, and stability.

Applying orthogonal finetuning beyond its original diffusion-model setting

outline.chapter_title: Limitations, Related Directions, and Future Work
outline.description: The closing chapter summarizes what BOFT achieves, clarifies its limitations, and points to open research questions. It also connects BOFT to adjacent lines of work on structured matrices, sparse training, and network topology design.
